p: At Ellie's game Jordan finally stood on the field where Danny collapsed, and found the defibrillator box before she found Ellie.
She planned her first solo cross country around the airspace shelves, with a turn point she named BEND, and filed a flight plan for each leg.
On the day she fixed a drifting gyro, flew around a snow shower on the side away from Denver, and landed behind a jet at the Colorado Air and Space Port, the one everybody calls the Space Port.
For three and a half hours she didn't think about Danny once. She felt guilty, then read his page about his own first cross country and let it go.
Walt told her eight months were gone and four were left, and that he was starting to think he'd be wrong about her.
Abby Strand. Jordan's instructor, who called the snow shower detour textbook.
Marisol Tran. The mechanic, who tests everything twice.
Walt Herrera. The club's safety officer, a dispatcher for thirty years.
Lourdes Reyes. Jordan's mother. Her birthday is in December.
Claire Reyes. Danny's widow, who passes on Ellie's questions about Greeley.

Abby had called on Sunday night, late, which Abby never did, after she'd read the cross-country log twice. She'd gone through it line by line, and then she'd moved on without a breath. Next is night. Three hours of it, ten full stops, one cross-country over a hundred miles. Then the long solo, a hundred and fifty and three stops, and you pick the route. A pause on the line. Not Greeley. It smells.

Monday, November 23, eleven at night, the station kitchen, a quiet hour on a twenty four. Jordan had Abby's list on a sticky note stuck to the station laptop and the regulations open on its screen, which was against some policy nobody had ever explained to her.
Her mother's text had come in at 6:15 and she'd been carrying it around all shift like a stone in a shoe.
A text from Lourdes Reyes. Sunday the 13th. Velarde's at 6:30. Same as always. Claire is driving me and the baby. You come too.

Velarde's was in Pueblo. It had been in Pueblo since before her mother was born there, a long room with red vinyl booths and a back room that the family took over on the Saturday nearest December 13 most years, and on December 13 itself when it fell on a weekend, whether or not the restaurant had planned on it. Her mother would be sixty three. It would be the first birthday without Danny.

And Danny had flown to it. Every year since he got his certificate, he'd flown Biscuit or a rental down to Pueblo Memorial, and somebody's cousin had picked him up in a truck, and Lourdes had sat in the back room with her phone face up on the table next to her plate until it buzzed. Jordan had driven. Every year. She'd been the one who brought the cake in the trunk.

She pulled up the chart on the laptop and measured it with the cursor because she didn't have the plotter with her. Centennial to Pueblo by I-25, about 80 miles. There and back, 160. Over a hundred. She looked at it for a while, the way you look at a number on a monitor you've already decided you don't like.
A text from Jordan Reyes. What if the night cross-country is Pueblo. Sunday Dec 13. Down at 5:15, back at 9.
Abby answered at 11:10, which meant Abby was also awake for reasons.
A text from Abby Strand. Pueblo's 80. Round trip 160. It works on paper. What's in Pueblo.
A text from Jordan Reyes. My mom's birthday dinner. Danny always flew down.

Three dots from Abby for a long time. Then: Ok. Then you have a deadline and a reason, which is two more things than the airplane needs. We'll talk about that. Night one is Wednesday. Be at the hangar at 4:15. Before sunset. I mean it.
Claire texted at 11:30, because apparently nobody in her life slept. El wants to know if she can ride down in Biscuit with you. I said ask Aunt Jordan. I'm sorry.

She wrote back the rule, because it was easier than the rest of it. Training flights don't carry passengers. And when I'm alone, student pilots can't. Not even El. Claire sent back a picture of Ellie's face reading the text, which said everything about the regulation that needed saying.

Later, at two, with the rig restocked and nobody calling, she took the green notebook out of her flight bag and paged through the back half. She wasn't looking for anything. Then she was. December, five years ago. The first line said KPUB, and Ma, and a number that would have been her mother's age. She didn't read the rest. She folded the corner down, the way she'd done with his first cross-country, and put the notebook back in the bag. His, after hers. That was the rule.

Wednesday, November 25, 4:15 PM, the ramp. Low sun on the foothills. The hangar shadows reached clear across the taxiway and onto the grass. Jordan had slept until one. Thursday at seven she was back at the station for Thanksgiving, which on an ambulance is a normal shift plus a pie somebody's mother drops off at the bay door around noon.

Abby came out of the office with two flashlights. One was the size of a baguette, with a red lens on a little hinge that flipped down over the white one. The other hung on a lanyard and smelled faintly of Abby's car, which was coffee and old fries.

Sunset's 4:38. Twilight ends 5:07. We take off before that and land after, which is the point of tonight. Six full stops. And the examiner is going to ask you what you did with the next half hour, so.
She checked her watch. Looked at the sky. Looked at Jordan.

She does the walkaround with the white light anyway, for the practice, while there's still daylight to check it against. Master on. Beacon, strobes, landing light. Red on the left wingtip, green on the right, white on the tail. Abby shows her the knuckle tap on each position light, and none of them so much as blink. Then she climbs in, turns the panel lights down to a dull orange, flips the red lens over, and sits. Abby sits. Nobody talks. Ten minutes in, the ramp starts coming back to her in grays, tie down rings, chocks, a gas cap somebody left sitting on a wing two rows over. There. Night eyes. Now don't look at your phone. I mean it. It's a flashlight with opinions.

The AFH recommends checking every light during the preflight and tapping the position light fixtures. Full dark adaptation takes about 30 minutes, moderate adaptation about 20 under dim red light, and any bright light for a second or more costs some of it.

First takeoff at 4:58, into a sky the color of a bruise. First landing at 5:05, technically a day landing, though it didn't feel like one. By the third takeoff it was night by the logbook's definition. Off three five right and right for the downwind, the runway slid back under the wing, and then there was nothing in the windshield at all.

East, out the left window, the subdivisions just stopped, like somebody had run out of houses. Past them was the plains, black, with ranch lights sprinkled on it here and there, and above the ranch lights, stars, and it was hard to say exactly where one bunch quit and the other started. The moon was coming up too. Huge, orange, ninety eight percent, sitting on the ground like a dropped plate.
Off the wing a string of headlights ran uphill across her window. She rolled level with it. Felt fine.

Attitude indicator. Ten degrees of right bank she hadn't felt and hadn't asked for. She rolls level, checks 6,900 on the altimeter, and right away the airplane swears to her it's banking left. She lets it swear. That's the road. Road's on a hill. Classic false horizon, and you'll get it every single time you turn east out here. Jordan says it out loud so it'll stick. Road's on a hill. Get it printed on a mug.
A dark scene with ground lights and stars, or a line of lights on sloping ground, can create a false horizon. The fix is the flight instruments for attitude, with the outside scan for traffic.

Fourth landing. Niner One Echo, runway three five right, cleared to land. She read it back. On base the approach lights were doing their thing, a little white rabbit running at the runway over and over, and the runway was a pair of white rows with a green bar at her end. Left side, a bit down, the PAPI.
Problem was, it looked right there. She'd hung on to her altitude on base an extra few seconds because of that, and now on final the PAPI said three white and one red. Then four white.
10,000 feet of runway. Abby had her chin on her fist and was looking out her side like she was thinking about lunch.

Little high, Jordan said. So fix it. She takes a hundred RPM out and leaves 65 where it is, and Biscuit sinks a bit, and the box goes three white and then two and two. There. Now quit touching it. Jordan puts the hundred back. Then she waits for the landing light to find the tire marks. It takes forever. Black rubber, finally, smeared across the white, and she starts the round out. On the rollout Abby says, Bright runway, dark ground. Gets everybody. Got me at Grand Junction my first winter, and I had eight hundred hours.

Three white and one red is slightly high on a four-light PAPI. A small power reduction at constant airspeed captures the glide path. AFH: round out when the landing light shows the tire marks on the runway.

After the first night she'd added a line to the bottom of the card on the panel, smaller than the rest because she was out of room. NIGHT: DUAL ONLY. CEILING 5,000 AGL ALL THE WAY. NO SNOW. NO RIDGES UNDER A LOWERING DECK. IF THE LIGHTS GO FUZZY, TURN AROUND.

Thursday, December 3, 7:40 PM. Night two. She'd come off a shift at seven that morning and slept until two, and had decided, out loud, in her kitchen, that she was fine, and had then made herself answer every letter of IMSAFE before she believed it. No moon tonight. It wouldn't be up until almost three in the morning. Abby had picked the night on purpose.

It was minus six on the ramp. Light leaked out where the hangar door didn't quite meet the frame. Inside, somebody was singing with the radio, badly. Marisol, then, fixing something that wasn't broken.

On the walkaround, master on, Jordan tapped the red light on the left wingtip with one knuckle, the way she had the first night. It went out. She tapped it again. It came on. Again. Out. It stayed out.

Marisol comes out in a headlamp with a spare bulb held in her teeth. The screwdriver comes out of a pocket Jordan didn't know the coveralls had. Two screws, lens off. The old bulb is scorched black on one side and the contact has gone fuzzy green. There's your blink. A wire brush, a new bulb, and then Jordan has to knock on it ten times while Marisol counts out loud. It stays on. Then the logbook, under the hangar light: date, tach time, lamp replaced, socket cleaned, signature, and the pencil goes back behind her ear. Danny tapped them too. Said the airplane would tell you things if you knocked.

The AFH recommends tapping position light fixtures during the night preflight and finding the cause of any flicker before flight. Position lights are required for night VFR, so the fix and the maintenance record come before takeoff.

8:31 PM, the practice area just north of Bennett, about twenty miles northeast of Centennial, 7,500 feet. The ground out here was about 5,500 feet and almost entirely invisible. There were the lights of Bennett off to the south, a gas station on I-70, and a county road running north and south below them with a farm light at every mile like beads. Between the beads, nothing. Fields, presumably.

Abby had shown her the winds before they left: about 15 knots out of the north at this altitude. She'd also, earlier, made Jordan read the glide card taped inside the POH cover, Marisol's capitals on an index card.
Best glide sixty five knots. Flaps up. A mile and a half for every thousand feet above the ground, no wind.
Abby reached over and pulled the throttle to idle.
Engine failure. Talk to me. We stop at 6,500, a thousand above the ground, and go home.

Nose up, trim, 65. She puts the field off the nose, a dark rectangle a mile and change north with a farm light at its corner and the road running down its west side. Into the wind. Fuel selector both, mixture rich, carb heat on, mags both, primer in and locked. Nothing changes, because Abby's hand is on the throttle. Mayday, mayday, mayday, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, engine failure, twenty miles northeast of Centennial, landing in a field. She says it to the windshield, not the radio. Landing light on at 6,800 to test it. The beam goes out and finds nothing. At 6,500 Abby pushes the throttle in and the engine roars back like it was offended. You'd have made it. You'd have seen the stubble in time from about two hundred feet. That's all a landing light gives you.

AFH night engine failure: best glide, toward an unlighted area of known terrain near public access, into the wind, check the causes, announce the emergency, and use the landing light in time to see the terrain. Avoid the road itself, which may have wires.

9:08 PM. The Space Port's tower had closed at nine, and the airport sat out on the plains ahead of them inside the Bravo's notch, under the 70, its beacon turning white and green, white and green, and below it nothing. No runway. A black hole where an eight thousand foot runway was supposed to be.

Jordan had the Chart Supplement entry on her kneeboard, copied the night before. The runway lights were on a radio switch now, on the airport's common frequency, which she'd already tuned. She'd announced herself on it, eight miles east, inbound for runway 26.
Abby had her hands in her lap.

Click click click click click click click. The runway comes on all at once, two long lines of white drawn on the dark, the threshold green, and a pair of lights to the left of the near end, one red, one white. Two-light PAPI. One and one is on path. Write down the time. 9:08. Fifteen minutes from now they go out whether you're on final or not. Key them again on downwind. She does, at 9:15, and again on the next downwind, without being told.

AIM 2-1-8: key the microphone 7 times within 5 seconds to turn on all controlled lights at maximum intensity, adjust lower with 5 or 3 if desired. Lights stay on 15 minutes from the last activation, so key again near the field.

9:36 PM. Three miles west of the Space Port, climbing for home under the 70. Behind them the runway lights were still on, burning down the last of their fifteen minutes. Abby reached across and flipped the ALT half of the master off.
The ammeter needle slid left of center and stayed there, a steady discharge.
Alternator's dead. You're on the battery. Go.
Back in May, on a Saturday, with the cowling off and Marisol not looking up from her wire, Jordan had answered this exact question, a night flight over Limon. Easier with your feet on concrete.

Landing light off. GPS off. The second radio off. Panel lights down to the least she can read. She keeps one radio and the transponder. Denver Approach, Niner One Echo, alternator failure, returning to the Space Port, three miles west. She banks back east and the runway is right there, still lit, a minute or two left on its timer. She keys it again, seven clicks, on downwind. Abby flips the ALT back on as they turn final, because it's training and the landing light makes the landing easier to grade. Nearest suitable. At night that means lit. You picked the one you'd just keyed. That's the whole lesson.

AFH: after a generating system failure, immediately shed nonessential loads, notify ATC, and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport. Keep what you need for communication and the landing, including what it takes to activate the lights.

Monday, December 7, eleven in the morning, the hangar. Biscuit's cowling was off again. Marisol called it an oil seep. Walt, walking through with a coffee, called it a hobby. Jordan's logbook said 3.6 hours of night now and ten night landings, five from the Wednesday before Thanksgiving and five from last Thursday. One box left. The cross-country.
Marisol had the little red extinguisher out from under the left seat and was reading it. The gauge, the date, the fine print, all of it, the way some people read a cereal box at breakfast.

Pop quiz. Night, 7,500, out over the plains. You smell something hot. Then smoke out the bottom of the cowling, right here, and she pointed the extinguisher at the bottom of the engine, at the exhaust pipes and the fuel lines, and there's light under it, and it's not your landing light. It's orange. What do your hands do first?

Mixture to cutoff. Fuel selector off. Yep. She reaches in and pulls the mixture all the way out to show her, then puts a boot on the fuel selector on the floor, the sticky one. All the way to OFF, and feel it seat. She's the one that hangs up short of BOTH, so don't trust your hand, trust the click. Do it blind a few times. Mags? The AFH says leave them on so the engine burns off what's in the lines. Biscuit's checklist doesn't mention them. If the fire goes out, it stays out. No restart. Biscuit's checklist says master off third, so make your mayday before you get there. Then you're a glider, with a story. She sets the extinguisher on the wing. This one's for the cabin. Pin, aim low at the base, squeeze, sweep. Then crack a vent, because the stuff in there isn't great to breathe either.

AFH engine fire procedure, unless the POH directs otherwise: shut off fuel with the mixture at idle cutoff and the fuel selector off, leave the ignition on to burn the fuel in the lines, don't restart, and make a forced landing.
Thursday, December 10, four in the afternoon, the briefing room. The Pueblo nav log was done, two pages in pencil, and Walt had asked to see it, which Walt didn't do.

He'd read her November fuel column once already and initialed it. He read this one the way he'd read release paperwork for thirty years, one finger moving down the page. Night's different. You know the rule. I want to hear what you plan.

Her log said 80 miles each way by I-25, 118 knots south with the forecast tailwind and 92 coming home into it, 8 gallons an hour, a gallon for taxi and a gallon for the climb at each end. Biscuit's tanks held 40 usable.
What do you land with? And where's your alternate on the way home?

She shows him the bottom of the page, where she'd already done it. Full tanks, 40. Pueblo with about 32. Home with about 23 if nothing goes wrong. And the line she'd written for him, because she knew he'd ask: if the Divide is down coming home, Pueblo to Monument and back to Pueblo, plus 45, is about 16 gallons, and she'd leave Pueblo with 32. Walt reads it twice. Then he takes a pen out of his jacket and, under her numbers, in small square capitals, writes RELEASED. W.H. Old habit. That's the number I'd have wanted on a release.

A dispatcher's fuel plan covers the destination, an alternate, and the reserve. Planning the return so a turnaround at the worst point still leaves the 91.151 night reserve is the ACS fuel planning risk element done properly.

Sunday, December 13, 8:50 in the morning, her kitchen. Her mother's birthday. She'd texted happy birthday at 7:01 and gotten back Thank you mija. Drive safe if you drive., which was her mother's way of saying a great many things.

The weather, printed at 8:44. Centennial now: three four zero at six, ten miles, scattered at twelve thousand, minus three and minus eleven. The Centennial TAF: three four zero at eight, scattered at twelve thousand. From twenty one hundred Zulu, three six zero at ten, broken at eight thousand. From oh four hundred Zulu, zero three zero at twelve, four miles in light snow and mist, overcast at twenty five hundred. From oh nine hundred Zulu, two miles in light snow, overcast at twelve hundred. Pueblo's TAF: three two zero at eight, a few clouds at twelve thousand, and from oh two hundred Zulu, three four zero at ten, scattered at eight thousand. Winds at nine thousand: three four zero at thirteen, minus eight. And notes off the graphical forecast for the Front Range and the Palmer Divide: upslope developing this evening behind a cold front, ceilings lowering to one thousand to twenty five hundred above the ground with light snow, earliest over the Divide. Timing uncertain.

She did the conversion out loud. Zero four hundred Zulu on the 14th, minus seven, is nine o'clock tonight. Her plan had her leaving Pueblo at 8:40 and landing at Centennial at about 9:35. Right into it.
And the graphical forecast said the Divide went first. Timing uncertain.
The night line on the card over the mag switch said 5,000 AGL all the way. She'd written it after the first night, when nothing was riding on it.

She writes it on the nav log in red before she can talk herself out of it. 4:45 PM, NEWEST TAF, METARS, PIREPS. DIVIDE CEILING PER THE CARD, ALL THE WAY, BOTH WAYS. IF NOT, I DRIVE. LEAVE BY 5:15 EITHER WAY. She takes a picture and sends it to Abby, who sends back a thumbs up and then, a minute later, Also put the cake in your car now. Either way.

The PHAK and RMH recommend setting decision criteria before the pressure arrives. A decision point on the latest data, a specific weather test for the critical terrain, and a ready alternative are what make a no-go easy to carry out.
1:40 PM, and her mother called. Called, not texted. Jordan watched the screen through two rings before she picked up.

Claire says you're going to fly to my dinner. A pause. Your brother always flew. Every year I sat in the back room at Velarde's with my phone on the table, face up, next to the bread, and every year the waiters knew not to move it. Another pause, longer. I'm not telling you not to come. I want you there. I'm telling you about the phone.

Behind her mother's voice she could hear Claire's kitchen, a cabinet banging, Ellie somewhere asking something about whether there'd be the flan with the burnt part. They were leaving at three. Ellie had made a sign. Jordan knew about the sign because Ellie had sent her a picture of it at noon: WELCOME TO PUEBLO AUNT JORDAN, in purple, with an airplane on it that was clearly Biscuit, because the 4 in the tail number was backward.
Claire had texted underneath the picture. She wants to watch you land. I told her maybe.

Ma. I might drive. Weather's coming over the Divide tonight, and I decide at quarter to five. Either way I'm there. If I drive I'm late, and I'll call when I leave. The line goes quiet. Then: Okay. Then, in a voice Jordan hasn't heard out of her since high school: Your brother never once told me maybe. Same text to Claire, plus: tell El the sign works for a car. Claire: Told her. She's adding a car. It has like nine wheels.

The PHAK lists managing passengers' and other people's expectations as a key way to manage external pressure. Telling the people waiting, ahead of time, that you might be late or drive takes away the pressure to make the flight happen.

4:45 PM. Biscuit's left seat, at the tie down, preflight done in the last of the light, every light tapped twice, the tanks topped to the filler necks. Abby in the right seat with the iPad on her knee. Overhead, the overcast was high and still gray-white. To the south, over the Palmer Divide, it wasn't. It was a flat gray lid sitting low on the ridgeline, and the ridgeline was gone under it in places.

The weather, printed at 4:41. Centennial: north at ten, ten miles, broken at five thousand, overcast at seven thousand. Colorado Springs: zero one zero at twelve, five miles in light snow and mist, overcast at twenty eight hundred. Pueblo: three three zero at nine, ten miles, scattered at eight thousand. Centennial's TAF, amended: from oh one hundred Zulu, four miles in light snow, overcast at two thousand. From oh four hundred Zulu, a mile and a half in light snow, overcast at eight hundred. And a pilot report from a Cessna 182 at twenty three twenty Zulu, ten miles north of the Black Forest VOR at eighty five hundred: overcast at ten thousand, flight visibility four miles in light snow, ceilings lowering rapidly, terrain obscured east of I-25.

She did the arithmetic the way she'd do a dose, one number at a time. The amended TAF brought the lowering at Centennial from nine o'clock to six. The PIREP was from a Skylane twenty five minutes ago, ten miles north of the Black Forest VOR, right over the top of the Divide: overcast at 10,000, flight visibility four in light snow, ceiling lowering rapidly. The ground under that airplane was about 7,500 feet. Twenty five hundred feet between the ridge and the clouds, and getting smaller. Colorado Springs had a 2,800 foot overcast and snow. Pueblo was fine. Pueblo was always going to be fine.

She looked at the card above the mag switch, at the small line she'd squeezed in at the bottom after the first night. CEILING 5,000 AGL ALL THE WAY. NO SNOW. NO RIDGES UNDER A LOWERING DECK. And above it, in bigger letters, the line she'd written in November. I DON'T CHANGE THIS CARD IN THE PARKING LOT.
Your call tonight, Abby said. It's legal right now, every piece of it. I'll fly what you decide. I'll tell you afterward what I'd have done.

No. It comes out easier than she expected, and quieter. The Divide's at 2,500 and dropping. That's not a number I'm crossing at night. I'm driving. Abby nods once, short, the nod she saves for a good checklist, and starts unbuckling. I'd have said no at four. I wanted to hear you say it. Jordan calls Claire from the cockpit, and Claire says Okay. I'll tell her. Drive safe, the pass is getting bad, and somewhere behind her Ellie shouts something about the car part of the sign.

The PIREP showed ceilings lowering rapidly over the highest terrain on the route, the TAF had been amended earlier, and it was night. The AFH says night VFR belongs in unrestricted visibility. Deciding on the ground, with a ready alternative, is the whole job.

Abby walked her to the hangar. Neither of them said anything about the flight that wasn't going to happen, which Jordan understood was a kind of respect. The tanks were full. They'd stay full. Russ had Biscuit Monday, and Russ would be delighted.

Walt was in the hangar. He hadn't said he'd be there. He was sitting on Marisol's rolling stool, the way he had in August with Russ's loading sheet on his knee, in his canvas jacket with two coffees from the FBO on the workbench beside him and his reading glasses folded in his shirt pocket. He'd been watching the weather on his phone, the way he must have watched it for thirty years, and he'd seen the PIREP. He'd known it was her night. He held out one of the coffees.

You're not going, he said. It wasn't a question, and he didn't sound pleased or surprised. He sounded like a man who'd been waiting at a gate to see which way somebody would walk. Sit down a minute before you drive. There's something I've been not telling you since April.
She sat on an upturned bucket. Walt looked at the coffee instead of at her.

Winter of ninety six. I was thirty four. Two years on the desk at a regional outfit that doesn't exist anymore. A thirty-some seat turboprop, eleven people in the back. A night run into a mountain town I'm not going to name. The forecast at the destination was above minimums, with snow showers in the vicinity. Legal. The alternate was legal. The fuel was legal, and then some. On an airline, the captain and the dispatcher both sign the release. Both of us own it.

I had a feeling about those showers. I didn't have a reason. I had a feeling, and a forecast that said yes, and a station that kept calling because there were people waiting for a wedding. So I signed. The captain signed. He turned the cup a quarter turn on the bench. They didn't come home.
The hangar heater ticked. Somewhere outside, a truck went by on the service road with its chains on.

The report said what those reports say. It talked about the descent and the snow and the terrain. It didn't have my name in it. It didn't need to. The release did. He finally looked at her. I've spent thirty years since then telling people things they didn't want to hear about the weather. I told myself it was the job. It was the eleven people. The forecast is permission. That's all it ever is. I treated it like a reason.

I wanted the share sold because I didn't think you'd be able to do what you just did. Most people can't. Most pilots can't. Your brother couldn't, and I loved your brother. He stood, slowly, the way he did everything. You turned it down with the tanks full and your family waiting. I've spent thirty years waiting to see somebody do that without me telling them to.
He picked up his coffee and went out the side door to his truck, and didn't look back, and Jordan understood that was the only way he could have said any of it.

Car running, heater on high and doing nothing yet, snow collecting in the corners of the windshield where the wipers didn't reach. She dug the green notebook out of her flight bag. Folded corner. His, after hers. She'd made her call, so now he got his.

Danny's logbook, a page from December, five years ago. Dec 11. KPUB to KAPA, night. 1.1 on the Hobbs. Ma's 58th at Velarde's. Left at 9:40 because Tia wouldn't stop bringing flan. TAF said the snow came after midnight. It came at ten. By Pueblo it was nothing, by the Springs it was low, by Monument it was the road. Followed the I-25 headlights over the hill at what I am going to write down as 800 feet and was not 800 feet. Lost the ground. I don't know how long. Long enough to know what it feels like. Came out over Larkspur with the wings level only because I was too scared to move them. Landed. Sat in the car an hour with the engine running. Called Ma from the car and told her it was a beautiful night. Got lucky. Never again. Don't tell Mom. (Next year leave Velarde's by 7. Beat it home.)

Twice through. Then the parentheses again, because of course. Never again, and one line down, how to keep doing it anyway. Leave by 7, beat it home. Every year after that he left a little earlier, and her mother thought it was because he worked in the morning.

She didn't start the wipers. Half an hour ago she'd been sitting in his airplane looking south at his ridge, same lid on it, same snow coming. And she'd turned around at the tie down. Which, it turned out, was the cheap place to do it.

She sat there furious with him, the snow filling in the glass, and for once she let herself have it. He'd called their mother from a parking lot and told her it was a beautiful night. He got lucky on that hill and kept flying it every December, just earlier, like the clock was the problem, and then he died on a Saturday morning of the one thing nobody could have turned around for.
Her mother wasn't getting the page. Don't tell Mom. Okay, Danny. Fine. She could do that one.
She called to say she was leaving instead. 5:20 on the dash clock. First ring.
I'm driving, Ma. I'm leaving now. I'll be late.
A long silence. Then: Okay. Go slow on the hill. They're saying it's bad on the hill.

Her mother was right about the hill. Past Castle Rock the snow came straight into the headlights, every semi had its flashers going, and somewhere ahead a plow kept throwing orange light across the median. Thirty five, both hands, radio off, a Subaru riding her bumper for six miles until it gave up. Once, near the top, she looked up at the ridge and the gray sitting on it and thought about a Skylane at 8,500 under that. Then road again.

Twenty after seven when she got to Velarde's. Somebody had propped the back room door open with a chair and it was still about ninety degrees in there. Green chile, an aunt's perfume, a space heater nobody could find the switch for. Balloons on the last chair, one already sagging. Ellie's sign was by the door, one corner already curling off the tape. Airplane, backward 4. Below it, added this afternoon in a purple from some other marker, a car with wings.

Her mother had the head of the table and the good maroon cardigan, sixty three as of this morning, and hadn't touched her enchiladas. The phone lay face up by the bread basket. Eleven years of waiters had known to leave it there.

For a while her mother just looked at her. A cousin at the far end quit talking mid-story. Jordan was still in the doorway, dripping, holding the cake box out with both hands like a delivery she needed signed for.

Her mother flipped the phone. Screen down on the tablecloth, next to the bread. Half the table missed it, and the half that saw it mostly thought she was being polite. Somebody's uncle wanted to know who'd called. Claire had a hand pressed flat over her mouth.

Eleven years I've sat at this table waiting for one of my kids to come down out of the sky, her mother said, to nobody in particular, to all of them. This is the first time one of my kids ever turned around.

Jordan didn't say anything. Her coat was dripping on the floor. She got the cake down a second before Ellie hit her in the knees, already mid-question. Did the car part work. Was it upslope, because Mom said upslope on the phone like twice. Was Biscuit scared. Yes, yes, and no, she's tied down, and on a night like this that's about the best a plane can hope for. Ellie took that in and asked when the flan was coming.

Flan, finally. Ellie got the burnt part, which had been negotiated in the car. Candles, then the song, English first, and on the Spanish verse the waiters came in so loud a busboy dropped a fork. Somewhere in there her mother reached over and took Jordan's hand on the tablecloth. She kept it through the coffee, eating left handed to do it. Nobody mentioned it.
At 10:52 PM, in her aunt's spare room, with an alarm set for 4:30 so she could follow the plows home and make the station by seven, her phone buzzed.

A text from Abby Strand. Rebooked. Wednesday the 16th, Pueblo, night cross-country, clear and cold all day. Your mother can have a second birthday. Then the long solo, then the written. Book the test for January. You're ready for it. You were ready for tonight too, which is the part that matters.
